(Ed. note: Hemp has been shut out of the greatest period of technological progress in human history. Consequently, it is fascinating to read about the development of technologies that have been frozen in time for more than half a century. This is one such story.)

The Modern Hemp Decorticator

The following interview was published in Hemp Magazine, Issue 20, November 1997, page 11

A NEW ERA

Decorticate: To strip or remove the bark, husk or outer covering of a plant.

Jim Hill is the founder and owner of Hill Agra Sales, a Canadian based company that manufactures and distributes bulk vegetable harvesting machinery. After sixty years of Marijuana prohibition, he has developed a working model of a decorticator, a machine for breaking and combing the hurds from the hemp stalks. this makes it possible to process more hemp fiber faster and finer than existing methods.

Hemp Magazine: How did you become an equipment manufacturer?

Jim Hill: I grew up with it. My dad bought the local blacksmith shop in 1950 and moved us from Toronto when I was seven. My job was working around the forge, pumping water to keep the kettles filled up; I’d watch all the neighborhood dogs come through and drink all the water. I grew up in the shop, learning all the different aspects of the trade. In 1959, I started working full time. There was a change from bags to bulk harvesting of potatoes and other root crop vegetables. I helped develop machinery to deal with the changes going on. We developed conveyors, graders, harvesters and bulk boxes for transport. Over the years, I just moved from one thing to another.

HM: Did you attend college to learn machining?

JH: No, I learned from the old white haired boys. I didn’t make a lot of my own mistakes until later on, I was a good listener and they were good teachers.

HM: Was Hill Agra Sales your father’s company?

JH: No, I started it. My dad’s name was Oscar Hill. All through the 50’s we were manufacturing all these machines. In 1969, I purchased his company and we started on expanding and exporting machinery down to the states and a few other countries.

HM: What would you estimate your physical sales for ‘96?

JH: In ‘96, sales weren’t really that good. We actually cut back on a lot of our production because the market is getting filled with this kind of equipment. But out sales were somewhere around a million dollars.

HM: How did you become interested in the decorticator?

JH: After building all kinds of general equipment for bulk processing, we moved into the field of more specialized machinery. We’ve built a whole array of machines production line companies could never have gotten to. I cut the number of men working for me down from forty to about eight or nine at a given time.

A few years ago, I spoke with some people who got me interested in the hemp industry. I read some of the books, magazines and papers; it was quite a mystery novel to me , and it got me to thinking. I just realized that this was an up and coming industry, hemp being just one of the fibers in question now. What we found, is that there have been no new developments in this industry for decades. Nothing new has been done in the flax industry for forty years. As for hemp, everything just dropped out in ‘38 with the prohibition. So, after researching the situation, and seeing several attempts at decorticating, I kept coming back to this point that the machine will do a lot of different things.

Not only will it decorticate the material for fabric, but the hurds that come out of it as a by-product, are a very useful commodity. Theoretically, if you had three tons of hemp per acre, one ton would be fiber. The other two tons would be a by-product that can be used for everything from animal bedding to wood products to absorption materials or paper making.

HM: So that’s the cornerstone of the argument for the decorticator versus the older method of field retting.

JH: In the old country, back in the Ukraine, the best method for separating the fiber

from the hurds, which is the stalk of the plant, was to rot it. The fastest method was to put it in water. Let it sit there and have the enzymes work on it for a while. You would take it out and let it dry until it turns to a silvery gray color. Then you had to stretch it between two pieces of wood and hit it in the middle with a third piece of wood to break it. After you break it, you take a course comb and comb the broken pieces of stalk out of the fibres inside the stalk. The hurds that were left were useless except as field fertilizer. It was a lot of hard work for not much fibre. This produces retted, or rotten hemp.

With the method that Schlichtin used, he was able to take field dried hemp, put it through his machine and a keep the fibre and the hurds at a nice consistent yellow color. This is unretted hemp. The unretted hurds are usable in making paper, so there is really no reason for retting hemp, but you have to remember that there are two crops coming out of this crop.

There is an early fibre and a late fibre. The early fibre is harvested at about 90 days of growth before the seed pods form. The late harvest yields not only the seeds, but also a courser grade of fibre and hurds. The process at this point is to cut and stook this material in the field. Instead of cutting it and rolling it like bales of hay, it is better to handle it like cane. This allows the plant to dry naturally, store easily and it doesn’t discolor the hurds.

HM: Why does the hurd color matter?

JH: You need fewer chemicals from the lighter material and remember that one acre of hemp equals about 4.1 acres of trees. When you decorticate the hemp, then you have two cash crops to sell and the value of 3 tons of hemp in the ground is increased dramatically.

HM: How did you come up with your design?

JH: Basically, what I have done is to study the Schlichtin papers, patents, and drawings. The way that machine is drawn up, there is no possible way that the machine could work based on that drawing. Back in those days, people changed their drawings from the original machine so they couldn’t be copied. They never trusted anybody. They had so many curves in the papers, that only someone who was very mechanically inclined could actually figure out what they were doing.

Every time I look at that patent, I can read new things into it. It is very well conceived and deceiving. The original machine that he built required four people to operate. That was two people putting the stalks in at one end, one person shoveling the hurds out from underneath, and a fourth person who had to be a good mechanic in order to keep the machine working. There were no bearings. The thing probably sounded like a flock of canaries when it was running. So, between oiling it and keeping the hemp from tangling up in the shafts, he was a very busy fellow.

HM: How is your design an improvement on the original?

JH: Our main goal was to maintain all the advantages he had built into his unit; such things as holding the rollers apart from one another, and having them spring loaded. This allowed you to adjust the height between the contact points in the rollers. Obviously, we had to put a high grade bearing in and have it protected against a rapping up in the fibres going through. Instead of putting an inside bearing, we put an external bearing that actually has its shaft continue over the mounting plate. This means that there is no chance of getting fibres caught in the bearing.

HM: How does it actually work?

JH: There are three steps. First, you split the stalk to expose the hurds. Then you

break the hurds, and finally, you comb the hurds out of the fibre. You put the stalks in at one end through a pair of indenting rollers. The stalks go through a set of spreading rollers, which are small disks. The disks are in a spring-loaded assembly and work against each other. Next comes the first breaking roller, which breaks the stalks in sections about an inch long. The second breaking roller breaks these pieces in half. The next assembly is a comb. It’s like sickle bar, only there are six of them on a shaft turning about 90 rpms. That combs out any hurds that are stuck in the fibre. The next roller is a slowspeed roller at about 30 rpms. Then it goes through a finer comb that also spins at 90 rpms. What you get out of the machine, are long fibres, short fibres, hurds, and a fine dust that is the glue and resin crystals from the stalks.

HM: How many people does it take to operate your machine:
JH: Two people can run it. Operating this machine is more just a question ofwatching it to make sure the material flows smoothly. It can be hand fed, or machine fed. There are all kinds of developments that can be added to this machine. The hurds that come out underneath the machine can be dropped on a conveyor and blown off into large plastic bags for later use. Our idea for the decorticator is that it should be used out in the field. This puts the dust right back in the ground for fertilizer. This also eliminates the ventilation problem you would have in a closed building.

HM: Is there a working model?

JH: We have it working, and it does what we expect of it. The machine is two feet wide and eight feet long. It is on a two-wheel trailer with jacks on either end. It is

hydraulically driven. The high and low speed rollers have variable speed controls with flow dividers. It can be run by a tractor of 60 horse power using the hydraulic pump on the tractor.

HM: What is the level of performance?

JH: This machine will do approximately a ton per hour. We could build machines

four or five feet wide and increase production up to two or three tonnes per hour. We have worked on other design for fibre extraction. The Schlichtin model is only one of several which we have been working on.

HM: Would this technology apply to other bast fibres?

JH: Absolutely. Almost every plant has fibre in it. It just depends on the fibres as to whether we can use them. Hemp is the strongest fibre, but we are not limited to hemp with this machine. We may have to change the indenting rollers and the combs depending on how fine a fibre we want. The procedure that we have reinvented (the new technology), is working very well. I’ve seen a lot of things come and go, and I predict that this fibre business is going to take hold and bring a lot of business into both of our countries.

HM: What do you see in the future?

JH: One of the largest industries hasn’t even been tapped into yet. And that is the automobile industry, and fibres. You start with a thickness of about three inches, spray on some resins, put it in a hot mold and press it, and it can make the interior pieces, the dashboard, fenders, or any other metal piece. This has already been happening in Europe for about five years. Volvo, Mercedes and Fiat replace steel components with this type of fibre. The automotive industry will be doing more of this in Canada and the U.S. because of the strength of the fibre. It is also totally biodregradable. That’s why they have done it.

HM: After the decorticator, what is the next most important piece of machinery to be built?

JH: It has to be the harvester. We want to be able to handle this plant like cane rather than like grass. We need to cut and stook it to let dry in the fields until decortication time. The decorticator is portable, so you can move it from field to field instead of moving all the material to a central location for processing. That means that several growers can get together and buy the equipment and handle this as any other crop.

After that, you can handle the product output in many different ways. You can upgrade your product at the farm gate and have that value ready to ship out as goods. This will allow the growers to realize more of the profit available from their crop.

HM: Well, let’s get started then!

JH: We’re ready.
